Maladaptive Strategies.value: try hard not think about the trauma
I throw myself into work or tasks to keep my mind occupied

Threat.value: I react with alarm when someone touches me unexpectedly
I always choose where to sit based on how safe or protected I feel

Memory.value: When the memory comes back it feels completely real across all my senses at once
There are parts of the event that I simply cannot remember no matter how hard I try
Remembering the event brings back the same terror I felt at the time

I should have protected others and I failed

issues.explanation: Pain Recall implies the patient personally sustained bodily injury during the trauma, which is hard to reconcile with the trauma type being trauma to a loved one unless there was also direct physical injury to the patient. That is not otherwise supported by the profile.

Physical Vulnerability and permanent bodily damage imply the patient believes his own body was physically harmed. For a trauma-to-a-loved-one presentation, this is difficult to explain clinically without evidence that he was also directly injured.

Military Topics is a trigger that suggests a military/combat-linked trauma context, but no other trigger, memory, threat, or appraisal item supports a military-related formulation. As a standalone item it feels disconnected from the rest of the profile.

Avoid Driving is plausible for motor-vehicle trauma, but here it lacks support from the trauma type and from the rest of the profile. With no transport-related trigger or memory content, it appears to target a symptom domain not otherwise represented.

For trauma to a loved one, visible injuries is a plausible trigger, but darkness and alcohol smell are not well anchored to the rest of the profile. Nothing in memory, threat, or appraisals suggests a dark-space or alcohol-related trauma context, so these triggers feel disconnected rather than part of a coherent loved-one trauma presentation.

Avoiding work/study is hard to reconcile with this patient's occupation as a paramedic unless the trauma is clearly tied to the workplace, but the rest of the profile frames the trauma as harm to a loved one rather than occupational trauma. Drug use is also insufficiently supported elsewhere in the profile: there are no other items indicating broad externalising coping or substance-related trigger context, making this strategy feel tacked on.

issues.item: Maladaptive Strategies: Avoid Work or Study: Going to work or study
issues.explanation: Self-blame can occur after trauma to a loved one, but this specific wording implies a direct causal role in the event. The rest of the profile does not provide supporting content suggesting he believes his own actions caused the loved one's trauma. The other appraisals are about damage and unreliability of self, so this item is the least integrated with the stated trauma type and surrounding node content.

Alcohol smell is not impossible, but in this profile it is the only trigger that suggests a substance-related context. The other trigger and memory items center on victims/injuries, which fits a paramedic exposed to injured loved ones or victims. Without any corresponding memory, threat, or appraisal content linked to alcohol, this item stands out as weakly connected to the rest of the trauma representation.

issues.item: Maladaptive Strategies: Drug Use: take drugs
issues.explanation: Drug use can occur in PTSD, but here it is the only maladaptive strategy that implies substance misuse. The rest of the profile emphasizes work avoidance, suppression, sensory reliving, and hypervigilant threat responses. With no parallel alcohol/substance-related trigger, appraisal, or memory content, this item looks clinically disconnected from the rest of the formulation.

issues.item: Negative Appraisals: Self-Blame: The event happened because of the way I acted
issues.explanation: For trauma to a loved one, self-blame is plausible only if the patient had a clear perceived role in failing to protect or respond. In this profile, the other items describe reliving of victims/injuries, hypervigilance, and damaged-self beliefs, but nothing else indicates a responsibility-based trauma narrative. This makes the specific self-blame item the least coherent appraisal relative to the rest of the selected content.

vignette: Ahmed, a forty-year-old paramedic of Lebanese descent, had always prided himself on the steadiness of his hands and the calm of his mind on the ambulance bay. His wife, Mariam, and their two children keep the house humming, but the quiet of their home has become a backdrop to a growing unease. In March, when he was called to a three-story residential fire, the tragedy that unfolded there would haunt him for years. A burst pipe had turned the living room into a maze of slick concrete and falling timber. He found his younger brother, Karim, trapped under a collapsed sofa, blood gushing from a shattered rib cage. Ahmed's first instinct was to extricate him, but the fire's heat and the smell of burning wood overwhelmed his efforts. He pulled Karim to a shallow safety zone, but the boy's eyes had already gone dim. The paramedics who arrived later took Karim to the emergency department, the antiseptic scent of the hospital lingering as he watched the ambulance door shut behind him. He had failed to save him. That day left Ahmed with a constellation of sensations: the sight of visible injuries on a loved one, the sharp, metallic taste of antiseptic, and the memory of the boy's last breath. Whenever he now passes by a casualty ward, the visual reminder of a wounded body triggers a flood of terror. The mere sight of a wound, the whiff of antiseptic, or even the flash of a blood-stained bandage sets his heart racing. The triggers ignite his maladaptive strategies-he suppresses the thought of that day, overworks at the station to keep his mind on the next call, and avoids any patient or scene that might resemble his brother's injuries. He no longer attends mandatory training sessions, citing exhaustion. The visual cues also heighten his threat reactions: a sudden touch from a colleague's hand sends him flinching as if a blade were behind it, and he insists on choosing the most "secure" seats in meetings, preferring the back corner where he feels protected. The same triggers summon vivid sensory memories of the fire, causing him to relive every crackling flame, every splintering splinter of wood, as though it were the present. In these moments, he experiences the terror of that night again, the same primal fear he felt when the house was still ablaze. The memories, in turn, reinforce Ahmed's negative appraisals. Each intrusive recollection confirms that he is permanently damaged, that he can no longer trust himself to act when danger is present. The guilt that his brother's life could have been saved feels like a permanent scar on his conscience, a failure that he cannot shake. These appraisals drive him further into avoidance and overwork. Believing he has failed, he tries to compensate by working harder, hoping that relentless effort will prove his worth. Yet, the more he works, the more his mind is forced to suppress the past, and the more his startle responses become frequent, even to benign touches. The fear of being hurt again amplifies his sensitivity to any trigger-an accidental glance at a wound, the echo of a hospital corridor, the faint smell of antiseptic. Each of these cues pulls him deeper into a cycle of avoidance, threat, and memory that feels impossible to escape. When Ahmed's coworkers notice he sits alone at the break room, he attributes it to his need for safety, but in reality, the avoidance is a response to the trigger of visual injuries and the threat of sudden contact. The avoidance itself feeds his memory intrusions: the isolation forces his mind to replay the scene, to imagine the crack of a splinter in the back of a hospital bed. The reliving, with its full sensory detail, increases his sense of failure and makes him feel even more incapable. Overworking, intended to keep his mind busy, paradoxically creates space for the intrusive images, because each pause is an invitation for the memory to surface. The threat reactions-being startled by a touch or losing concentration-are not just reactions to the present; they are amplified by the sense that his body is still in a state of emergency, always on guard. Every time he feels a threat, his self-efficacy erodes further, reinforcing the belief that he cannot rely on himself. His belief that he failed to protect his brother makes him more attuned to potential threats; he scans the ambulance bay for anything that might resemble a dangerous scene, even when none is present. Thus, his maladaptive strategies, memory, threat, and negative appraisals are locked together, each pulling the other into a tightening loop that leaves him exhausted, paranoid, and increasingly isolated. The cycle has taken a toll on Ahmed's life. He no longer volunteers for night shifts, fearing the possibility of an emergency involving a wounded loved one. His wife, concerned, has urged him to see a therapist, but Ahmed has resisted, convinced that staying in the field will prove his worth. Yet the relentless cycle of avoidance and overwork has made his work performance slip, and he has missed key procedural updates. The fear that he might again fail, combined with the knowledge that his avoidance is harming his career, is what finally pushes him to seek help. Ahmed now stands at a crossroad: he hopes to reclaim a sense of control over his body's reactions, to trust himself again, and to stop fearing that one more glance at a wound will bring back the terror of that night. He is terrified that the cycle will persist, that he will continue to be unable to rely on himself, and that his sense of permanent damage will never ease. In his own words, he longs for a way to stop being haunted by his brother's death and to find a space where he can function without the constant, paralyzing threat that haunts every trigger.
